newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FEATURE - Ireland wants EMU - with or without Britain.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ireland wants EMU - with or without Britain.

text.p: Ireland is sticking to guidelines for European economic and monetary union (EMU) and has remained committed to the single currency ever since it ratified the Maastricht Treaty in 1992 without an opt-out clause.
But as launch date for EMU draws ever closer in January 1999, fears of repercussions on Irish business if Ireland joins without its main trading partner -- Britain -- are mounting.

Intra-party unity on monetary union has remained unwavering within the Irish government and unlike most European aspirants, the country has not needed to struggle to meet the tough entry requirements.

Its low-inflation economy is booming, boasting the fastest growth rate in Europe for the last four years. The country's gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate hit double digits in 1995, running at 10.7 percent year-on-year -- which compares with an average EU growth rate of roughly two percent.

Ireland is one of the few European Union members whose debt-to-GDP ratio is already comfortably within the three perent EMU entry limit, while its overall debt-to-GDP ratio is sinking fast enough to satisfy EMU planners.
Ireland also has the will of its people pushing it towards Europe. In 1972, 83 percent of its 3.5 million population voted in favour of joining Europe.
JOINING WITHOUT BRITAIN SEEN AS POSSIBLE

Although concerns have become more vociferous of late, a recent survey of Irish business still shows wide acceptance that Ireland would be worse off it it stays out of EMU with Britain than if it joins the union without its bigger neighbor.
"Staying out of EMU, as far as we are concerned, is more likely to give higher Irish interest rates and an unstable exchange rate," a spokesman for Ireland's Central Bank told Reuters.

"We are working within a framework that we are going into EMU and the acceptance of Maastricht is not conditional on what Britain and sterling do," the spokesman said. "But that is not to say that we would not prefer to have sterling in."
The risk for Ireland entering EMU without Britain is that it will be highly exposed to sterling volatility, trapped within the confines of a single currency without control over its exchange rate.
Ireland's official trade statistics show a sharp reduction in dependence on Britain in the last 25 years but the statistics are not showing the whole story.

In 1970, 66 percent of Irish exports were exported to Britain with only 12 percent going to the rest of Europe. In 1995, official trade data showed only 26 percent of Irish exports destined for Britain and 47 percent going to Europe.
The problem is the statistics are skewed by multinational transactions.

Multi-national corporations currently account for half of all exports out of Ireland. These large transnational operations use Ireland as a backdoor to Europe and have little trade with Britain. This makes Ireland's dependence on Britain look artificially low.
The bulk of indigenous Irish manufacturing exports are still going to Britain and their dependence on sterling is great.
So why doesn't Ireland take a risk averse view and follow Britain rather than Europe?
Ireland has made many attempts to break its dependence on its former ruler. It decoupled from sterling, breaking its one-to-one link, in 1989.
Since then Ireland has made great efforts to be a "good European", struggling to keep the Irish currency at a credible level within the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

"If Ireland was to stay outside EMU it is arguable that we could be in a vulnerable and isolated position," Ireland's central bank governor Maurice O'Connell told the recent European Finance Convention in Dublin.
"The markets would question our motives. The Irish pound might carry a significant interest rate premium," he said.
Staying out could also impact on inward investment, he warned.
"One has to ask whether an Ireland semi-detached from the heart of Europe would remain such an attractive location for new overseas investment," O'Connell said.
He also felt that Ireland may find it considerably more difficult down the road to satisfy EMU criteria. "These are serious downsides that we should not underestimate."
Finance minister Ruairi Quinn has articulated similar sentiment.

"If we were to be outside the euro and declared to the rest of the world that we were qualifying to join a single currency but we were deciding for whatever reason not to join it, largely because of our dependence on sterling, I think we would compound our vulnerability," Quinn told Reuters in a recent interview.
LITTLE CONCRETE PREPARATION FOR EMU
Notwithstanding this relatively unanimous drive towards Europe, Ireland has changed little of a statutory nature or otherwise to underpin its committment.
A survey of Irish business showed that little or no effort was being made to accomodate the possibility of EMU occurring.

Even Ireland's 1996 Central Bank Bill, which is currently going through parliament, makes no reference to special EMU requirements which require prospective members to make statutory provisions to allow its central bank full independence.
The European Commission and European Monetary Institute (EMI) will assess whether each central bank fulfills such EU rules in early 1998.
The Irish central bank spokesman said that while nothing had yet been changed, once the EMI produced a full menu of requirements the central bank would swiftly incorporate them.

"When this year's bill was being prepared there was talk about making some EMU related changes that were reasonably obvious but as it became clear that the EMI was still examining the issue and we did not yet know all the changes that would be needed," the central bank spokesman said.
"So it was decided that we would leave specifically EMU-related issues aside until the full menu was known," he said.
